extracted.intended_audience: young or inexperienced housekeepers and domestic cooks (mistresses supervising household servants)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, prescriptive guidance for running a household kitchen and preparing a wide range of recipes (soups, meats, pickles, preserves, puddings, etc.), with instructions on organization, economy, and technique aimed at the domestic manager/cook. Includes both high-level household-management rules and detailed recipe/process specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodical household management (three rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The grand arcanum of management lies in three simple rules: 'Let every thing be done at a proper time, keep every thing in its proper place, and put every thing to its proper use.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce a regular system into each department, examine different departments each morning to detect errors early, and modify systems until matured and then enforce them as inviolable law. Method reduces labour and expense by using proper proportions and predictable routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early rising and punctual breakfasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Early rising is essential to the good government of a family; a late breakfast deranges the whole business of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require each person to be ready at breakfast (avoid 'breakfast by detachments'); mistress should use servants' breakfast time to do light tasks (wash cups, arrange cruets) so the day proceeds without delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistress prepares and measures ingredients for servants
rubrics_metrics.description: The mistress must give out every thing intended for the dinner in proper quantities—butter, sugar, flour, meal, lard, catsup, spice, wine—measured to the cook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This saves waste and prevents temptation or carelessness by subordinates; it relieves the mistress from constant interruptions during the day. Expecting servants to remember all small items leads to inefficiency and waste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy through accurate weights and measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce labour and be economical: when ingredients are given in just proportions the article made is always equally good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipes and household accounts should be reduced to proper weights and measures by experiment; consistent proportions prevent waste and variable quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily inspection to catch small errors early
rubrics_metrics.description: If the mistress every morning examines minutely the different departments of her household, she must detect errors in their infant state, when they can be corrected with ease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small neglect left a few days grows into disorder; early detection prevents 'gigantic' problems. Implies routine checklists and daily supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skimming and gentle simmering for clear soups
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let the pot boil over; take off the scum carefully as it rises; keep it gently and steadily boiling for hours to leave clear soup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making beef/stock soups, maintain steady gentle heat for many hours, remove scum, and avoid boiling over. For some ingredients (thyme, celery), add near the end to preserve delicate flavour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for adding delicate herbs and ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: Add thyme, parsley, celery, or other delicate ingredients later in the cooking (e.g., after four hours) so they do not lose delicate flavour or discolour the soup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delicate herbs would lose their flavour if boiled too long. For oysters and other delicate items, add at the end and cook only until just done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thickening soups without curdling
rubrics_metrics.description: Thicken soups with a mixture of flour, butter, milk (or cream), and sometimes the yolks of eggs beaten well; if cream is not perfectly sweet and eggs not quite new, the thickening will curdle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strain the egg/cream/flour mixture, add some hot soup by degrees while stirring, then return to pot and boil briefly to remove raw taste. Take care that flour is in fine state and that mixture does not form lumps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Browning soups using caramelized sugar
rubrics_metrics.description: Brown soup by melting a small spoonful of nice brown sugar in an iron skillet until very dark, then stir in ladlefuls of soup and strain this browning back into the soup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This produces rich colour and flavour; stir constantly to avoid burning; strain to remove solids. Used as final step before serving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting butchers' meat (quality indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: To choose butchers' meat, see that the fat is not yellow; the lean parts should be of a fine close grain, a lively colour, and feel tender when pinched; poultry should be well covered with white fat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid meat where fat has a tinge of yellow (sign of disease or old age). Best age for beef is three to five years; larger oxen are coarser. Color/texture/fat are primary selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curing beef: brine proportions and process
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare brine with one pound of saltpetre powdered, fifteen quarts of salt, and fifteen gallons of cold water; stir until dissolved—this brine will be strong enough to bear up an egg.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rub fresh-killed beef thoroughly with salt, let lie in salt ten days, brush off, wipe, then put into brine with weight to keep under. Keep brine in cool dry place, skim dross; use proper tubs with holes to let bloody brine run off. Tongues cure similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drying beef for summer use (storage & handling)
rubrics_metrics.description: After salting and brining (specified times), wipe pieces dry, rub with bran, and hang in a cool, dry, dark place suspended so they do not touch anything; inspect occasionally and sun after wet weather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dried meats must be soaked in water the night before use. In boiling dried meat use large quantity of water, start from cold water, boil steadily and skim until bones are ready to fall out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corned beef in hot weather (quick cure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rub a thin brisket with two large spoonsful of pounded saltpetre, pour on a gill of molasses and a quart of salt, rub them in and let it sit in a vessel just large enough to hold it (allow bloody brine to run off); in four days it can be boiled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep vessel not tight to allow runoff; if possible, keep in a refrigerator/ice-house. Same method works for veal fillet or mutton leg.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roasting technique and presentation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Soak meat in water one hour, wipe dry, set before a clear, steady fire; baste initially with salt and water, then with good lard in the dripping-pan; cover with paper while browning, then remove, dredge with flour, turn quickly and baste to raise a froth. Veal/lamb/pork need more roasting; beef and mutton less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not run the spit through the nice parts; skin and peel mutton as directed; serve beef and mutton without sauce (garnish with horseradish); if gravy is desired, serve in a boat. Avoid visible dry flour on meat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiling meats (start in cold salted water)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is to be boiled must be put into cold water with a little salt so they cook regularly; putting meat into boiling water cooks the outside too much before the inside heats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boil steadily, skim pot, continue until bones fall out or skin peels easily. Use lots of water for dried meat to rehydrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer lard over butter for basting and frying
rubrics_metrics.description: Nice lard is much better than butter for basting roasted meats, or for frying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lard for its performance at high heat and flavour for many savory applications; butter may be used sparingly for veal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using gross or overly strong parts of fowl for some dishes
rubrics_metrics.description: When making soup from old fowl: separate the breast from the ribs and throw away the back (too gross and strong for use); remove skin and fat from gross parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For old fowl, feed in a 'coop' before slaughter to improve edibility; use only the nicer parts for soups and ragouts; trim away overly gross tissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent curdling in cream-and-egg thickenings
rubrics_metrics.description: If the cream be not perfectly sweet, and the eggs quite new, the thickening will curdle in the soup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure fresh eggs and sweet cream; warm and mix the cream/flour/yolks gradually with hot soup before returning to pot; stir continuously and boil briefly to set, avoiding overheating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of verification signs during curing (brine 'bear up an egg')
rubrics_metrics.description: This brine will be strong enough to bear up an egg: if more salt be added it will fall to the bottom without strengthening the brine, the water being already saturated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'egg floats' test to verify brine strength; observe and correct concentrations by stirring and skimming; timing (mid-October start) and storage (cool dry place) affect outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of delicate seafood and shellfish
rubrics_metrics.description: For oyster soup: wash and drain oysters; first reduce a larger quantity, then add fresh oysters near the end; thicken and serve, taking care that it does not curdle and that flour is not in lumps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overcook oysters; strain when needed; optional thyme may be added sparingly but not boiled long enough to discolor the soup.
